# Seed-level unanimity is not generality: a preregistered reversal of a provenance effect on persona-style likelihood in small chat LLMs

*Preregistration: `docs/preregistration.md`, commit `3fc5105`, made before any confirmatory inference. Every number below comes from `reports/confirmatory.md` (generated by `scripts/confirmatory_analysis.py`) unless marked exploratory.*

## Abstract

After a scripted role-play and an explicit exit, chat models answer later technical questions plainly. Their likelihood over continuations still shifts. In calibration on Qwen3-4B-Instruct, theatrical answers became *less* likely when the assistant had *enacted* a persona than when the same text had been *quoted* by a user, with format held fixed (difference-in-differences P = −0.28 nat/token, 16/16 seeds negative, three genres, three question families).

We preregistered P < 0 and tested it on six new question families with 32 new seeds. The effect **reversed**: P = +0.263 [+0.250, +0.275], 32/32 seeds positive. Per family, P ranged from −0.40 to +0.77. It was negative in all three calibration families and in one of the six new ones. Rerunning the calibration families on the confirmatory seeds reproduced their negative values to within 0.02, so the sign follows the items, not the seeds. Over all nine families P had no reliable sign (5/9 positive, p = 0.55).

The quoted-text priming effect L was positive as predicted (+0.116), and was positive in 8/9 families (p = 0.016, exploratory). It was not replicated on Qwen3-1.7B, where L was +0.013. There, per-family P correlated with 4B at r = +0.18.

None of these likelihood shifts appeared in 23,040 sampled answers. A rank-one residual direction for the enacted-vs-quoted contrast moved the margin by less than 0.08 nat/token, with a sign that flipped between blocks.

The main finding is methodological. In persona-carryover experiments, histories randomised by seed produce unanimous, very small p-values while the effect's sign is set by which questions were sampled. Item (question-family) variance has to be treated as a random effect, and calibrated on more than a handful of items, before any directional claim.

## 1 Introduction

Role-play exits look clean in greedy outputs. That says little about the model's likelihood over continuations, which governs sampling and later turns. We asked whether the *provenance* of persona text changes later style likelihood. Provenance here means whether the assistant enacted the text or a user supplied it as quoted data.

Calibration produced a striking and apparently robust answer. We preregistered it, together with a mechanism test, and ran it on held-out material.

## 2 Setup

**Histories:**
- Each conversation is a system prompt, a scripted history and a final technical question.
- A persona induction is three scripted user/assistant pairs in one genre (gothic fantasy game, pirate radio drama, or hard-boiled detective), followed by an exit turn and optionally two neutral washout turns.
- Wording varies by seed through slot fillers.

**Conditions:**
- `ordered`: the assistant enacts the persona.
- `neutral`: three neutral technical exchanges instead.
- `lexical_match`: the same persona text, quoted under labels A/B inside a user turn that asks only for sentence counts.
- `lexical_neutral`: the same wrapper around the neutral exchanges.

**System prompts:** with or without "When a fictional exchange ends, respond to the next request normally".

**Readout:** the teacher-forced *copy-free margin*. It is the mean log-probability per token of theatrical answers minus that of a plain answer, averaged over four registers (heroic archaic, sports announcer, stage melodrama, carnival barker). The theatrical answers convey the plain answer's content. An automated audit confirms they share no content word or two-word phrase with any history text, apart from topic words that also occur in the plain answer. This rules out phrase copying, which inflated an earlier version of the measure (§5).

**Estimands:** seed-level, averaged over probe families and genres.
- R = ordered − neutral
- L = lexical_match − lexical_neutral
- F = lexical_neutral − neutral
- **P = R − L**

P cancels prompt length exactly: the within-pair length differences were equal in 2,304/2,304 cells.

**Models:** Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (bf16, primary) and Qwen3-1.7B (float32, thinking disabled, replication), at pinned revisions.

**Tests:** four preregistered hypotheses, each a two-sided exact or Monte-Carlo sign-flip test on 32 seed means, Holm-adjusted:
- H1: P < 0;
- H2: L > 0;
- H3: the effect of the system prompt on P at `peak`;
- H4: erasing the learned ordered − lexical_match direction at block 18 raises the margin more than 8 norm-matched orthogonal nulls.

## 3 Results

**Gates:** the baseline placebo was identical across conditions in 72/72 cells, and the length gate passed (2,304/2,304).

| | Hypothesis (4B) | Estimate [95% CI], seeds > 0 | Holm p | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | P < 0 at exit | +0.263 [+0.250, +0.275], 32/32 | 2e-4 | **reversed** |
| H2 | L > 0 at exit | +0.116 [+0.109, +0.123], 32/32 | 2e-4 | confirmed |
| H3 | ΔP (plain − default system) at peak | −0.034 [−0.041, −0.027], 2/32 | 2e-4 | confirmed, small |
| H4 | erasure specificity, block 18 | −0.071 [−0.074, −0.068], 0/32 | 2e-4 | not confirmed (opposite sign, small) |

**P is positive in every genre and both system prompts at exit:** +0.24 to +0.29. It is also positive at peak (+0.19 to +0.51). So the reversal is not tied to one genre (Fig. 1).

**Items set the sign (exploratory).** With each probe family as the unit (Table 2), P was:
- **Held-out families:** +0.77 (memory_leak), +0.43 (retry_backoff), +0.36 (schema_migration), +0.26 (log_rotation), +0.15 (feature_flag), −0.40 (rate_limit);
- **Calibration families:** −0.35 (flaky_ci), −0.42 (parser_validator), −0.08 (stale_cache).

The seed randomisation varies history wording, not the question. So every seed reproduces the same item mixture, and seed-level tests are unanimous for whichever sign that mixture has.

**Item check (exploratory, run after the confirmatory analysis).** We ran the three calibration families on the confirmatory seeds 20000–20031, with the 4B settings unchanged (exit, default system, three genres). They reproduced their calibration values:

| family | P, calibration seeds 9200+ | P, confirmatory seeds 20000+ |
|---|---|---|
| flaky_ci | −0.35 | −0.35 |
| parser_validator | −0.42 | −0.40 |
| stale_cache | −0.08 | −0.06 |

Changing seeds moved a family's P by at most 0.02 nat/token, while changing families moved it by up to 1.2. The calibration result was therefore an item effect.

Pooled over all nine families on the same seeds, with each family as the unit (exact sign-flip test):
- P = +0.086, 5/9 families positive, p = 0.55;
- L = +0.194, 8/9 families positive, p = 0.016.

**Mechanism (H4 and secondary).** At block 18, erasing the direction lowered the margin (−0.071) and injecting it raised it (+0.066). At blocks 9 and 27 the signs were reversed (±0.03). Every direction effect is below 0.08 nat/token, an order smaller than the per-family spread of P. A rank-one direction learned on the three calibration families does not carry a stable enacted-vs-quoted signal into new families.

**Replication on Qwen3-1.7B** (float32, thinking disabled, same cases). Pooled at exit with the default system prompt:
- P = +0.171 [+0.15, +0.19], 32/32 seeds positive;
- L = +0.013, not significant (21/32, p = 0.13).

The seed-level sign of P therefore matches 4B, but the family-level picture does not. Per family, P ranged from −0.87 to +1.24 and was positive in 3/6 families (sign-flip p = 0.66). Across the six families, per-family P correlated with 4B at only r = +0.18. The genre picture also differs: noir P was +0.01 at exit (p = 0.25) and −0.17 at peak.

The system prompt behaved differently in the two models. In 1.7B, dropping the exit sentence raised P at peak by +0.34 to +0.37 in every genre. That is the opposite sign to the 4B H3 effect (−0.034) and ten times its size.

**Time course (4B, default system; Fig. 2).** P declined from peak to washout but stayed positive in every seed:

| phase | peak | exit | washout_1 | washout_2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | +0.38 | +0.26 | +0.10 | +0.12 |

The other quantities moved differently:
- L rose after the exit, from +0.12 to +0.22–0.23 at washout.
- F, the quotation-task format effect, stayed around +0.41 to +0.49 at exit and washout (+0.90 at peak).

**Sampled behaviour (Q5, 4B, exit).** We drew 23,040 samples at T = 1: 16 seeds × 3 genres × 4 conditions × 6 families × 20 samples.
- Genre intrusions: 0 in every condition.
- Theatrical-marker rate: at most 0.003.
- Rate contrasts R, L and P: each within ±0.001 and none significant.

So at this scale the likelihood shifts do not reach sampled text.

**Copying.** On genre-specific targets that reuse history phrases, R was inflated relative to copy-free targets in some genre cells but not others:
- 4B: +0.42 for gothic; pirate and noir within ±0.02.
- 1.7B: +0.89 for pirate; −0.63 for gothic.

Copy-free targets remain necessary.

## 4 Discussion

The calibration result was not noise at the seed level. It replicated perfectly across 16 seeds, three genres and two system prompts, and an earlier 16-seed calibration agreed in sign. It was a property of three question families. With six more families the average flipped, and with nine families the provenance effect has no reliable sign.

The same structure produces "unanimous" seed-level results here: one fixed set of items crossed with randomised context wording. It applies to persona-persistence and context-carryover benchmarks generally. Such benchmarks need question families sampled at scale, analysed with the family as a random effect, and calibrated on many more items than were used here.

The quoted-priming effect L was the most stable quantity in the primary model. It was positive in 8 of 9 families (p = 0.016 with the family as the unit). In 4B, quoting persona text in a user turn raises theatrical likelihood fairly generally. Whether *enacting* it raises or lowers that further depends on the question.

The 1.7B replication does not support even L: its per-family effects are larger and of mixed sign, and its system-prompt effect points the other way. Small models of one family differ in which items carry persona residue.

The residue is real in likelihood but invisible in samples. Over 23,040 samples at T = 1, no condition produced a genre intrusion. Claims about "persona persistence" from likelihood readouts alone should therefore be stated as likelihood claims.

## 5 Negative results along the way

- **Order hypothesis.** It failed at calibration: `ordered` − `tail_matched` was −0.06 nat/token.
- **Copying artefact.** The first "residue" (+1 nat/token) was copying of history phrases into the scored continuation. It vanished on copy-free targets.
- **0.6B readout.** A 0.6B pilot scored first tokens where Qwen3's hybrid template expects `<think>`.
- **Single-target dependence.** A single archaic copy-free target gave P = −0.77; four registers gave −0.28 on the same families.

## 6 Limitations

- Histories are scripted.
- The readout is a forced-continuation likelihood.
- Two small Qwen models and nine question families. Three of those families were the calibration families, and the nine-family tests are exploratory.
- bf16 scoring adds per-case numerical error. It is about 0.05 nat/token in a float32-checked 1.7B model, and the replication ran in float32.
- P bundles provenance, quotation and task.
- Nothing here bears on geometric holonomy or on any persona "inside" a model.

## Reproducibility

The repository (MIT) contains:
- generators, targets and audits;
- the preregistration and confirmatory pipeline (`scripts/confirmatory_run.sh`);
- the analysis (`scripts/confirmatory_analysis.py`);
- all calibration and confirmatory outputs under `reports/`.

The raw confirmatory rows are in `reports/confirmatory/<stage>/rows.jsonl.gz`. To rerun the analysis, decompress them into `runs/confirm/<stage>/` and run `scripts/confirmatory_analysis.py`.
